newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: U.S. says Swiss bank boycott would be wrong move.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says Swiss bank boycott would be wrong move.

text.p: The head of a Clinton administration probe into Nazi assets on Thursday said a boycott of Swiss banks would be counterproductive to Switzerland's efforts to clear up its World War Two financial role.
Commerce Undersecretary Stuart Eizenstat, chairman of a United States interagency task force, said damage to the Swiss banking system would not be in the U.S. or world interest.
Eizenstat praised the Swiss government and banks for launching what he called a sincere effort to track lost Jewish accounts and probe Swiss financial ties with Nazi Germany.

"I don't want to talk about any particular city council's actions but in general this is not the time for confrontation, its a time for cooperation," Eizenstat told Reuters when asked about a New York City push to bar business with Swiss banks.

New York city and state warned on Wednesday they might bar government deposits with the banks or make it hard for them to do business in one of the world's top financial centres unless Switzerland compensates Holocaust survivors.

"Confrontation would be counterproductive, it would a set-back. It would be a way of saying that despite all of the efforts that they (the Swiss) have made over the last several months, that those efforts, far from being admired and rewarded, were being punished," Eizenstat said.

Swiss banks said earlier they took took the New York boycott threat seriously but were puzzled the proposal was made now after Swiss businesses and the government last week agreed to a humanitarian fund for victims of Nazi persecution.

Eizenstat, speaking after talks with Swiss bankers, politicians and local Jewish leaders, played down Swiss fears that a powerful push by world Jewish groups for compensation was in reality a plot to undermine their country.
"A strong Swiss banking system is essential to the health of the world economy," Eizenstat told a news conference.
Switzerland's three biggest banks -- Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS), Credit Suisse Group and Swiss Bank Corp (SBC) -- rank among the world's 20 biggest financial insitutes.

Eizenstat, whose task force is looking at what U.S. government documents can reveal about the flow of Nazi assets in wartime Switzerland and elsewhere, said its first preliminary report would be presented in mid or late March.

Eizenstat said he was encouraged by Swizterland's rapid creation of two commissions, one hunting for accounts left by Holocaust victims and the other looking at Swiss financial ties with Hitler's Germany, including the flow of assets from Holocaust victims and Nazis.

"We also welcome the declared intention of the Swiss government to establish an interim fund to compensate Holocaust victims," he said about an agreement last week between Berne and Swiss banks and businesses.

But Eizenstat made clear the U.S. was pushing for fast results from the Swiss probes and resulting action after months of criticism from Jewish groups and U.S. Senator Alfonse D'Amato that Switzerland profited cynically from the Holocaust.

Eizenstat said he would meet Swiss Foreign Minister Flavio Cotti at the Davos world economic summit on Friday and talk about "the sense of urgency that the commissions and reviews that have been set up report on a prompt basis".

In Geneva, U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan told a news conference on Thursday he viewed Switzerland's dispute with Jewish groups over the funds as a "public relations disaster" and urged a quick end to the row.
He was responding to a question on whether he thought Switzerland's perceived neutrality as host to the U.N.'s European headquarters had been compromised by the controversy.
